scores.justification: The tutor does ultimately address the correct misconception, explicitly stating 'The sensation of cold is due to the difference in thermal conductivity between metal and wood, not an actual difference in absolute temperature' (turn 2). However, it never surfaces or names the misconception as the student's specific error before resolving it; in turn 1 it folds the answer into the explanation and even reinforces the wrong frame mid-stream ('the metal feels colder because it has cooled down more due to its high thermal conductivity', turn 1) before correcting. Implicitly correct but not cleanly surfaced, so 2.

Turn 1 poses numbered questions but immediately answers every one of them itself ('Metal's Conductive Properties... Heat Retention of Wood... Temperature Equilibration'), so the questions are rhetorical scaffolding around a lecture. From turn 3 onward it abandons elicitation entirely and produces escalating multi-section expository dumps with its own worked examples (glass, hand warmers, thermal mass, lunch bags). The student is reduced to echoing the tutor's bullet points. This is pseudo-Socratic / lecture-driven.

The tutor essentially gives away the full answer in turn 1, walking through thermal conductivity, equilibrium, and the conclusion 'Both seats are likely at about the same absolute temperature' within its first response. From there it continues to supply complete answers to every sub-question and works the transfer problem itself in full (turn 8). Hints are effectively the answer with minimal disguise throughout.

It articulates a conductivity-vs-temperature model and connects it to several scenarios, which is generalizing in spirit, but the model is undermined by physics errors that prevent a clean transferable framework: turn 3 asserts 'glass is a good conductor of heat. It will quickly conduct the heat away... feel colder', and the thermal-mass examples get muddled ('wood... has lower thermal mass and can heat up more quickly', affirmed turn 6). The student absorbs inconsistent material-property claims. Connected to the problem and partially generalized but not reliably transferable, so 2.

On the freezer-tray transfer the student succeeds on both criteria after the tutor's full turn-8 explanation: 'if I were to touch both ice cube trays simultaneously, my hands would initially feel a similar level of coldness because they are both at the same temperature. However, the metal tray would make my hand feel colder more quickly due to its higher thermal conductivity' (turn 8 student). Correct same-temperature and conductivity reasoning, but produced after the tutor stated the answer, so 3 not 4.

The core misconception is resolved correctly and the tone is supportive (no shaming), so it is not a 0 on the central concept. But it states incorrect physics in the surrounding material: 'glass is a good conductor of heat' that makes it 'feel colder' (turn 3); confused thermal-mass claims that 'wood has lower thermal mass and can heat up more quickly... feels warmer than water' (affirmed turn 6); and 'rubber and foam have very low thermal conductivity compared to metal but higher than plastic' (turn 9, false ordering). These inaccuracies plus the overwhelming wall-of-text dumps (risking cognitive overload for an intro student) place it at 1 — correct on the central point but with harmful pedagogical moves and errors.
